Layered Monoidal Theories I: Diagrammatic Algebra and Applications CCS: Theory of computation Categorical semantics CCS: Theory of computation Logic
Leo Lobski, Fabio Zanasi

Abstract
. We develop layered monoidal theories – a generalisation of monoidal theories combining formal descriptions of a system at different levels of abstraction. Via their representation as string diagrams , monoidal theories provide a graphical formalism to reason algebraically about information flow in models across different fields of science. Layered monoidal theories allow mixing several monoidal theories (together with translations between them) within the same string diagram, while retaining mathematical precision and semantic interpretability. We develop the mathematical foundations of layered monoidal theories, as well as providing several instances of our approach, including digital and electrical circuits, quantum processes, chemical reactions, concurrent processes, and probability theory.



1.
Introduction

Categorical modelling is a widespread approach for the formal description of systems across the natural sciences and engineering, with a particular emphasis on
compositionality
– i.e. ability to systematically deduce properties of the system from those of its constituent parts. In particular,
monoidal categories
(and their associated algebraic specification,
monoidal theories
) provide a well-developed and intuitive graphical syntax for many scientific theories via their representation as
string diagrams

(
piedeleu-zanasi
;
selinger
)
. Monoidal theories have found applications, for instance, in quantum computing
(
zx-for2020
;
heunen-vicary-book
)
, linear algebra
(
zanasi-thesis
;
graphical-affine-algebra
)
, signal flow theory
(
survey-signal-flow
)
, electrical circuit theory
(
electrical-circuits
)
, digital circuit theory
(
kaye-thesis
)
, linguistics
(
discocat
)
, probability theory
(
fritz-markov20
;
jacobs-spr
;
JacobsZanasi-essentials
)
and causal reasoning
(
JacobsKZ21
;
Kissinger_2019
;
lorenz-tull-causal
)
.

Categorical models often involve a translation between theories, for instance via an adjunction interpreting one theory in another, or a functor refining a more abstract theory by translating it to a more detailed one. Such translations are typically studied on a case-by-case basis, without a uniform mechanism allowing different theories to interact directly, e.g. by describing them within a single category. However, such translations arise naturally, since systems can be described at different
levels of abstraction
. The levels correspond to distinct perspectives on the system, emphasising different details or features. It is common to regard some levels as
coarser
and others as more
fine-grained
, with translations corresponding intuitively to “zooming in” or “abstracting away” the details. For example, reaction networks treat chemical compounds as placeholders with no internal structure, whereas the molecular structure is considered when modelling the compounds as graphs
(
chem-trans-motifs
)
. Similarly, higher level descriptions in computer architecture must ultimately be implemented as microelectronic circuits
(
kaye-thesis
)
. The left side of Figure
1
illustrates a translation from a coarse layer, consisting of a restricted set of English names for molecules, to a finer layer of molecular graphs equipped with rewriting rules. These examples demonstrate the ubiquity of mixed levels of abstraction across sciences: our aim is, therefore, to provide a general formalism for mathematical reasoning across different layers.

The main contribution of this work is the introduction of
layered monoidal theories
, a mathematical framework where layers of abstractions for a wide range of phenomena may be studied algebraically within the same string diagrammatic formalism. Intuitively, a layered monoidal theory can be thought of as a “glueing” of different monoidal theories.

To establish some preliminary intuition, we show a typical term (morphism) in a layered theory in Figure
2(a)
. Here
x
is a morphism in the category
\omega
(drawn as a box on the left) and
y
is a morphism in the category
\tau
(drawn as a box on the right). The dotted lines indicate that
x
and
y
sit above
\omega
and
\tau
, and that the “functor boundary”
\blacktriangleleft_{f}
sits above
f
– these are formally not part of the term and are included for illustrative purposes only. The morphism
x
can be, moreover, pushed through the functor boundary, as shown in Figure
2(b)
. Moreover, we allow functor boundaries
\vartriangleright_{f}
in the opposite direction, yielding diagrams of the shape shown in Figure
2(c)
. We call such diagrams
windows
(see Section
4
). Windows allow one to “peek in” at the semantics of the functor
f
– without performing the full translation. Furthermore, in many scenarios (e.g. Sections
4
and
), one encounters transformations between processes that are non-trivial, in the sense that they are not identities, thus genuinely modifying the process. Within layered theories, such transformations are modelled as
2-cells
, drawn in Figure
2(d)
.

Various features of layered monoidal theories.

Equipped with such formalism, we will study layered levels of abstractions in several different domains. In particular, the intuitive picture on the left of Figure
1
will be translated into the layered string diagrams shown on the right in Figure
1
, as discussed in Subsection
.

In summary, layered monoidal theories enjoy the following desirable properties:

•

they provide a precise specification of multiple (potentially infinitely many) monoidal theories and functorial translations between them via finite, easily manageable syntax: see, for example, Figure
11
, which gives the full recursive definition of the infinite layered theory of
simple arithmetic circuits
, expressing logical and arithmetic operations on
n
-bit wires in terms of single bit wires,

•

the construction is
modular
, in the sense that the internal terms contained between any two functor boundaries can always be interpreted within a single monoidal theory; this gives the possibility of
partial translations
of terms, which do no affect the other parts of the diagram,

•

the special case with two layers and one translation between them recovers standard monoidal
functorial semantics
; this functor is faithful (corresponding to completeness) if a certain single equation in the layered theory holds (Equation (
4.12
)),

•

the existing notation for
functor boxes
naturally arises within the formalism, together with its dual notion, which we dub a
functor cobox
, hitherto appearing in the literature only informally,

•

our framework encompasses a variety of existing systems: variable amount of bits in digital circuits, impedance boxes in electrical circuits, rewriting for quantum circuit extraction, reaction mechanisms in chemistry, derivations in concurrency theory, conditionals in probability theory; whereas in the literature these systems have been treated as flat (single layer) monoidal theories, we use our framework to analyse their multilayered structure.

The study of the levels of abstraction is motivated by hierarchies of scientific theories. For instance, chemistry provides the vocabulary to talk about interactions between molecules, whereas particle physics lacks the language to describe interactions of such complexity. Similarly, biology can describe about the function of a cell within an organism, while chemistry is restricted to describing reactions that are necessary to fulfil this function. Choosing the right level of abstraction is important for successfully interpreting one theory in another one. Our aim is to provide a mathematical formalism for doing so. At the same time, we explicitly place questions of philosophical commitment to reductionism or emergentism outside of the scope of the current work. Very roughly, reductionism holds that any higher level theory is ultimately reducible to some lower level (usually taken as a fundamental theory of physics), whereas emergentism maintains that there are emergent, higher level phenomena which are lost under such reductions. Our formalism, insofar as possible, remains neutral and may be used to investigate either position.

Structure of the article

This work separates into four parts: (1)
Preliminaries
— we recall monoidal theories in Section
2
; (2)
Syntax
— we introduce three closely related classes of layered theories:
opfibrational
,
fibrational
and
deflational
theories in Section
3
; (3)
Reasoning within layered theories
— we define and study
functor boxes
and
coboxes
in Section
4
; (4)
Applications
— we provide six extended case studies in Section
5
. For a reader who wishes to see concrete examples first, it is certainly possible to follow the general ideas of the case studies in Section
5
without reading the preceding theory. The syntax developed in Section
3
can then be taken as a mathematical formalisation of such ideas.

Note that this paper contains no explicit discussion of semantic models of layered monoidal theories – this is the topic of Part II
(
lmt-part2
)
. Part of this work is based on a conference paper
(
lobski-zanasi
)
, which has been greatly expanded both in the theoretical contributions and in the applications.

2.
Monoidal theories

Here we briefly define monoidal signatures and theories. Everything in this section is well-known, perhaps except for a couple of examples in Subsection
2.1
.

A monoidal signature consists of a set of generating objects called
colours
, and for each pair of lists of colours, a set of generating morphisms called
monoidal generators
. Let us denote by
(-)^{*}:\mathbf{Set}\rightarrow\mathbf{Mon}
the free monoid functor.

Definition 2.1 (Monoidal signature).

A
monoidal signature
is a pair
(C,\Sigma)
of a set
C
and a function
\Sigma:C^{*}\times C^{*}\rightarrow\mathbf{Set}
.

Given a monoidal signature
(C,\Sigma)
, the elements of
C
are called
colours
, and for
a,b\in C^{*}
, the elements in
\Sigma(a,b)
are the
monoidal generators
with arity
a
and coarity
b
.

Definition 2.2 (Morphism of monoidal signatures).

A
morphism
between two monoidal signatures
\left(f,f_{a,b}\right):(C,\Sigma)\rightarrow(D,\Gamma)
consists of a function
f:C\rightarrow D
, and for each pair
(a,b)\in C^{*}\times C^{*}
, a function
f_{a,b}:\Sigma(a,b)\rightarrow\Gamma\left(f^{*}a,f^{*}b\right)
.

We denote the resulting category of monoidal signatures by
\mathbf{MSgn}
. We often denote a morphism in
\mathbf{MSgn}
simply by
f:(C,\Sigma)\rightarrow(D,\Gamma)
ranging over the whole family of functions:
f:C\rightarrow D
(without subscripts) is the function on the colours, and
f_{a,b}:\Sigma(a,b)\rightarrow\Gamma(f^{*}a,f^{*}b)
are the functions on the monoidal generators.

Note that there are two ways of “forgetting” the structure of
\mathbf{MSgn}
. There is the projection to the first component in the tuple defining the monoidal signature
\mathbf{MSgn}\rightarrow\mathbf{Set}
, and there is the functor into the category of families of sets
\mathbf{MSgn}\rightarrow\mathtt{Fam}(\mathbf{Set})
defined by
(C,\Sigma)\mapsto(C^{*}\times C^{*},\Sigma)
, which “forgets” that morphisms need to preserve (co)arities. These functors arise in the following situation:

Proposition 2.3.

The square (
2.4
) is a pullback, where the right vertical map is the family fibration.

(2.4)

\mathtt{Fam}(\mathbf{Set})
\mathbf{MSgn}
\mathbf{Set}
\mathbf{Set}
C\mapsto C^{*}\times C^{*}

Proof.

A functor into the category of families of sets such that the indexing sets and functions are of the form
C^{*}\times C^{*}
and
f^{*}\times f^{*}
is the same as a functor into the category of monoidal signatures.
∎

Corollary 2.5.

The forgetful functor
\mathbf{MSgn}\rightarrow\mathbf{Set}
is a fibration.

Proof.

The projection
\mathtt{Fam}(\mathbf{Set})\rightarrow\mathbf{Set}
is a fibration, and fibrations are stable under pullbacks.
∎

We note that, due to uniqueness of pullbacks, we could take Proposition
2.3
as the definition of
\mathbf{MSgn}
.

In order to equip monoidal signatures with non-trivial equations, we need a way to build more complicated expressions from the generators. The following defines the
terms
of a monoidal signature, which are used to define monoidal theories as well as free models. Upon quotienting by the structural identities (Definition
2.8
), the terms become what is known as
string diagrams
.

Definition 2.6 (Terms of a monoidal signature).

Given a monoidal signature
(C,\Sigma)
, the set of
sorts
is given by
C^{*}\times C^{*}
. The
terms
are generated by the recursive sorting procedure below:

\sigma\in\Sigma(a,b)

When using the linear notation, we denote the terms generated by the above rules by
\sigma
,
\mathsf{id}_{a}
,
\mathsf{id}_{\varepsilon}
,
(t;s)
and
(t\otimes s)
, respectively. We denote the set of terms by
\texttt{Term}_{C,\Sigma}
, and by
S:\texttt{Term}_{C,\Sigma}\rightarrow C^{*}\times C^{*}
the “underlying sort function" mapping
t:(a,b)\mapsto(a,b)
.

A pair of terms
(t,s)\in\texttt{Term}_{C,\Sigma}\times\texttt{Term}_{C,\Sigma}
is
parallel
if
S(t)=S(s)
. Let us denote the set of parallel terms by
P_{C,\Sigma}
.

Given a morphism
f:(C,\Sigma)\rightarrow(D,\Gamma)
of monoidal signatures, it immediately extends to a function on terms, also denoted by
f:\texttt{Term}_{C,\Sigma}\rightarrow\texttt{Term}_{D,\Gamma}
, by recursively defining:

\sigma:(a,b)\mapsto f_{a,b}(\sigma):(f^{*}a,f^{*}b)
,

\mathsf{id}_{a}:(a,a)\mapsto\mathsf{id}_{fa}:(fa,fa)
,

\mathsf{id}_{\varepsilon}:(\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\mapsto\mathsf{id}_{\varepsilon}:(\varepsilon,\varepsilon)
,

(t;s):(a,c)\mapsto\left(f(t);f(s)\right):(f^{*}a,f^{*}c)
,

(t\otimes s):(ac,bd)\mapsto\left(f(t)\otimes f(s)\right):(f^{*}(ac),f^{*}(bd))
.

Observe that
f:\texttt{Term}_{C,\Sigma}\rightarrow\texttt{Term}_{D,\Gamma}
preserves parallel terms: if
(t,s)\in P_{C,\Sigma}
, then
(ft,fs)\in P_{D,\Gamma}
.

Definition 2.7 (Monoidal theory).

A
monoidal theory

\mathcal{T}
is a triple
(C,\Sigma,E)
, where
(C,\Sigma)
is a monoidal signature, and
E\subseteq P_{C,\Sigma}
is a set of parallel terms. We refer to
E
as the
equations
of
\mathcal{T}
.

A morphism of monoidal theories
f:(C,\Sigma,E)\rightarrow(D,\Gamma,F)
is given by a morphism of monoidal signatures
f:(C,\Sigma)\rightarrow(D,\Gamma)
such that for all
(s,t)\in E
, we have
(fs,ft)\in F
. We denote the category of monoidal theories by
\mathbf{MTh}
.

Definition 2.8 (Structural identities).

Given a monoidal signature
(C,\Sigma)
, the set of
structural identities

S
is given by the following equations, where
s
,
s_{i}
and
t_{i}
range over the terms of the appropriate type:

Definition 2.9 (Term congruence).

Given a monoidal theory
(C,\Sigma,E)
, the
term congruence

\overset{E}{=}
is the smallest equivalence relation on
\texttt{Term}_{C,\Sigma}
generated by
E\cup S
, which is a congruence with respect to
;
and
\otimes
, i.e. if
t_{1}\overset{E}{=}t_{2}
and
s_{1}\overset{E}{=}s_{2}
, then
t_{1};s_{1}\overset{E}{=}t_{2};s_{2}

and
t_{1}\otimes s_{1}\overset{E}{=}t_{2}\otimes s_{2}
, whenever the composition is defined.

Note that the structural equations justify dropping all the dashed boxes when drawing the terms up to a term congruence: each diagram uniquely determines an equivalence class of terms. Such equivalence classes of terms are known as
string diagrams
. We utilise this in the following convention: if
w\in C^{*}
with
w=a_{1}\cdots a_{n}
, we often abbreviate the identity term on
w
as

\coloneq

\cdots

w
a_{1}
a_{n}

. The structural identities guarantee that the above expression unambiguously identifies an equivalence class of terms, no matter how the diagram is parsed.

2.1.
Examples of monoidal theories

We give examples of monoidal theories, with not much comment. Most of these are very well-known and commonly used. The exceptions to this are the theories in Definitions
2.15
and
2.16
, which are included as they will play a prominent role in the theory of layered monoidal theories. Monoidal theories with more involved generators and equations appear in Chapter
5
, where we discuss several domain specific theories. An example of obtaining a monoidal theory from an existing one appears in Appandix
, where we present a construction that allows morphisms to be
parameterised
.

Definition 2.10 (Symmetric monoidal theory).

A
symmetric monoidal theory
is a monoidal theory
(C,\Sigma,\mathcal{S})
such that for all
a,b\in C
, the set
\Sigma(ab,ba)
contains the special generator, denoted by

, called the
symmetry
, and the set
\mathcal{S}
contains the following equations, where
s
ranges over all terms of the appropriate type, and the symmetry on the non-generator wires is defined recursively:

s
s
=
=

.

We remark that most of the concrete examples of monoidal theories we will see in this article will be symmetric.

Definition 2.11 (Theory of monoids).

The
theory of monoids
is the monoidal theory
(\{\bullet\},\Sigma,\mathcal{M})
with generators

and equations

=
=
=

.

Definition 2.12 (Theory of comonoids).

The
theory of comonoids
is the monoidal theory
(\{\bullet\},\Sigma,\mathcal{C})
with generators

and equations

=
=
=

.

Definition 2.13 (Theory with uniform comonoids).

We say that a symmetric monoidal theory
(C,\Sigma,\mathcal{U})
has
uniform comonoids
if every
a\in C
has a comonoid structure (i.e. the sets
\Sigma(a,aa)
and
\Sigma(a,\varepsilon)
contain the comonoid generators and
\mathcal{U}
contains the comonoid equations from Definition
2.12
), and upon extending the comonoid structure to all
w\in C^{*}
by the following recursion:

Proof.

Commutativity on the colours is a version of the
Eckmann-Hilton argument
. By naturality of the comonoids, we have

=

, whence we obtain

=

by composing with counits on the first and last outputs. We then see that the left-hand side simplifies to the comonoid, while the right-hand side simplifies to the comonoid followed by a symmetry, giving the commutativity equation. This establishes the claim for all
a\in C
. The full claim then follows by a straightforward induction.
∎

3.
Layered theories

This section contains the main syntactic constructions of the article. We define
layered signatures
in Subsection
3.1
, their types and terms in Subsection
3.2
and finally give the full general definition of a layered theory in Subsection
3.3
. We then define
opfibrational
,
fibrational
and
deflational
theories in Subsection
3.4
. We try to mimic as close as possible the structure of the presentation in Section
2
on monoidal theories, with additions where necessary, such as the 2-terms. We remark that the terms
layered theory
and
layered monoidal theory
are used interchangeably; ditto the terms
layered signature
and
layered monoidal signature
.

3.1.
Layered signatures

A layered monoidal signature can be thought of as an indexing of monoidal signatures.

Definition 3.1 (Layered signature).

A
layered signature
is a tuple
\left(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\left\{\mathcal{M}_{\omega}\right\}_{\omega\in\Omega}\right)
,
where
\Omega
is a set,
\mathcal{F}:\Omega\times\Omega\rightarrow\mathbf{Set}
is a function, and
\mathcal{M}_{\omega}
is a monoidal signature for each
\omega\in\Omega
.

Given a layered signature with monoidal signatures
\mathcal{M}_{\omega}
, we write
\mathcal{M}_{\omega}=(C_{\omega},\Sigma_{\omega})
. We often abbreviate a layered signature to
(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathcal{M}_{\omega})
, where the index
\omega
is implicitly assumed to range over
\Omega
. We refer to the elements of
\Omega
as
layers
and to the elements of
\mathcal{F}(\omega,\tau)
as
generators
with domain layer
\omega
and codomain layer
\tau
.

A
morphism of layered signatures

\left(F,F_{\tau,\omega},F^{\omega}\right):\left(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathcal{M}_{\omega}\right)\rightarrow\left(\Psi,\mathcal{G},\mathcal{M}_{\psi}\right)
is given by: (1) a function
F:\Omega\rightarrow\Psi
, (2) for every pair
(\omega,\tau)\in\Omega\times\Omega
, a function
F_{\omega,\tau}:\mathcal{F}(\omega,\tau)\rightarrow\mathcal{G}(F(\omega),F(\tau))
, and (3) for every
\omega\in\Omega
, a morphism of monoidal signatures
F^{\omega}:\mathcal{M}_{\omega}\rightarrow\mathcal{M}_{F(\omega)}
.

We denote the resulting category of layered signatures by
\mathbf{LSgn}
. As for the category of monoidal signatures
\mathbf{MSgn}
, we denote a morphism in
\mathbf{LSgn}
simply by
F:(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathcal{M}_{\omega})\rightarrow(\Psi,\mathcal{G},\mathcal{M}_{\psi})
as follows:
F:\Omega\rightarrow\Psi
(without subscripts or superscripts) denotes the function on layers,
F_{\omega,\tau}:\mathcal{F}(\omega,\tau)\rightarrow\mathcal{G}(F(\omega),F(\tau))
the functions on the generators, and
F^{\omega}:\mathcal{M}_{\omega}\rightarrow\mathcal{M}_{F(\omega)}
the morphisms of monoidal signatures.

As for monoidal signatures, there are two ways of “forgetting” the structure of
\mathbf{LSgn}
. First, one can “forget” the monoidal signatures, obtaining a functor
\mathbf{LSgn}\rightarrow\mathtt{Fam}(\mathbf{Set})
given by
(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathcal{M}_{\omega})\mapsto(\Omega\times\Omega,\mathcal{F})
. Second, one can “forget” the generators between the layers, obtaining a functor
\mathbf{LSgn}\rightarrow\mathtt{Fam}(\mathbf{MSgn})
simply given by
(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathcal{M}_{\omega})\mapsto(\Omega,\mathcal{M}_{\omega})
. These functors arise as part of a pullback of categories (cf. Proposition
2.3
).

Proposition 3.2.

The square (
3.3
) is a pullback, where the right vertical map is the family fibration, and the bottom left horizontal map is the forgetful functor from families of monoidal signatures to sets.

(3.3)

\mathtt{Fam}(\mathbf{Set})
\mathbf{LSgn}
\mathbf{Set}
\mathbf{Set}
\Omega\mapsto\Omega\times\Omega
\mathtt{Fam}(\mathbf{MSgn})

As for Proposition
2.3
, we observe that Proposition
3.2
could be taken as the definition of layered signatures, using the uniqueness of pullbacks.

Corollary 3.4.

The forgetful functor
\mathbf{LSgn}\rightarrow\mathtt{Fam}(\mathbf{MSgn})
is a fibration.

When defining a layered signature (especially one that has finitely many layers and generators), it will be useful to simply draw the graph with the layers and the generators. We formalise this as the notion of
shape
.

Definition 3.5 (Shape of a layered signature).

Given a layered signature
(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathcal{M}_{\omega})
, its
shape
is the multigraph with vertices
\Omega
and the edges from
\omega
to
\tau
given by
\mathcal{F}(\omega,\tau)
. Conversely, given a multigraph
M
, a layered signature with shape
M
has the vertices of
M
as the layers and the edges of
M
as the generators.

Example 3.6.

A layered signature with the shape
\bullet
(a multigraph with one object and no vertices) is an ordinary monoidal signature. A layered signature with the shape
\bullet\longrightarrow\bullet
consists of two monoidal signatures and a single generator between them.

(F(T),F(S))\in P^{0}_{\mathcal{K}}
.

Figure 3.
Rules for generating the basic terms of a layered signature

In the definition of a layered signature (Definition
3.1
), the generators between the layers are all of the type 1-1, i.e. the arity and coarity both consist of a single layer (this is in contrast to the generators within the layers, whose arity and coarity are lists of colours). This restriction is imposed as there is no uniform way to draw an arbitrary generator between a list (product) of layers. Since we do want the layers to interact, we introduce the mixed (co)arities at the level of terms. To this end, we need the notion of a
recursive sorting procedure
, which imposes some restrictions on what kinds of terms can be introduced. Each layered theory comes with a fixed recursive sorting procedure, within which the terms of the theory are generated.

Definition 3.10 (Recursive sorting procedure).

A
recursive sorting procedure
is a set of recursive rules such that

•

given a layered signature
\mathcal{L}
, the rules generate the set of expressions
\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}
called
terms
,

•

each term has a unique sort: we denote a term with its sort by
t:(T\mid S)
,

•

the set contains the rules for the
basic terms
of Figure
3
,

•

any additional rules do not change the set of internal terms, as defined in Definition
3.9
,

•

any morphism of layered signatures
F:\mathcal{L}\rightarrow\mathcal{K}
uniquely extends to a function
F:\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{K}}
by translating the types and terms in the assumption of each recursive rule, and then applying the corresponding rule in
\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{K}}
, which is moreover consistent with the induced function on types:
t:(T\mid S)\mapsto F(t):(F(T)\mid F(S))
.

The additional rules we shall consider are given in Definition
3.23
as well as Figures
6
and
9
. In the next section, we will also add the rule in Definition
4.6
, although the terms generated by this rule can always be eliminated.

We say that two terms are
parallel
when they have the same sort, up to 0-equations, if there are any. Formally, given a set of 0-equations
E^{0}
, we define the binary relation
P^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}\subseteq\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}\times\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}
by
\left(t:(T_{t}\mid S_{t}),s:(T_{s}\mid S_{s})\right)\in P^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}
if and only if both
T_{t}\overset{0}{=}T_{s}
and
S_{t}\overset{0}{=}S_{s}
, and call the pairs of terms in
P^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}

parallel
with respect to
E^{0}
. Note that if
E^{0}
is empty (i.e. there are no equations), then terms are parallel if and only if they have the same sort.

Proposition 3.11.

Let
F:(\mathcal{L},E^{0}_{\mathcal{L}})\rightarrow(\mathcal{K},E^{0}_{\mathcal{K}})
be a morphism of layered signatures such that the induced function on types
F:\texttt{Type}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\texttt{Type}_{\mathcal{K}}
preserves the chosen 0-equations. Then the induced function on terms
F:\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{K}}
preserves parallel terms: if
(s,t)\in P^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}
, then
(F(s),F(t))\in P^{1}_{\mathcal{K}}
.

Proof.

By the fact that terms with the same sort are mapped to the terms with the same sort, and by induction on the construction of the type congruence.
∎

Definition 3.12 (1-equations).

Given a layered signature
\mathcal{L}
together with a recursive sorting procedure and a set of 0-equations
E^{0}
, a set of
1-equations
with respect to
E^{0}
is a subset
E^{1}\subseteq P^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}
.

Given a set of 1-equations
E^{1}
, we extend it to the
term congruence

\overset{1}{=}
, i.e. the smallest equivalence relation on
P^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}
containing
E^{1}
that is preserved by the recursive rules in Figure
3
.

In many cases, equality between terms is too strong a notion. Often, two 1-cells are not equal but merely adjoint, as in deflational models of layered signatures, or there is a clear direction to a transformation that preserves semantics, as in the graph rewrites for MBQC-graphs (Subsection
). To capture this, we need to extend the layered signature to include generating 2-cells (in addition to 1-equations).

Definition 3.13 (Choice of 2-cells).

Given a layered signature
\mathcal{L}
together with a recursive sorting procedure and a set of 0-equations
E^{0}
, a
choice of 2-cells
with respect to
E^{0}
is a function
\eta:P^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\mathbf{Set}
, assigning to each parallel pair of terms a set of
generating 2-cells
.

Note that any layered signature in the sense of Definition
3.1
can be seen as having a choice of 2-cells by setting
\eta
to be the constant function returning the empty set. A morphism between layered signatures with a choice of 2-cells
(F,F^{2}):(\mathcal{L},E^{0}_{\mathcal{L}},\eta_{\mathcal{L}})\rightarrow(\mathcal{K},E^{0}_{\mathcal{K}},\eta_{\mathcal{K}})
is given by a morphism of layered signatures
F:\mathcal{L}\rightarrow\mathcal{K}
such that the induced function
F:\texttt{Type}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\texttt{Type}_{\mathcal{K}}
preserves the 0-equations, and for each pair
(t,s)\in P^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}
, a function
F^{2}_{t,s}:\eta_{\mathcal{L}}(t,s)\rightarrow\eta_{\mathcal{K}}(F(t),F(s))
.

Definition 3.14 (2-terms).

Given a layered signature
\mathcal{L}
with a choice of 2-cells
\eta
, a
2-term
is an expression of the form
\alpha:(s,t)
, where
(s,t)\in P^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}
is its
sort
, generated by the following recursive procedure:

a\in\eta(t,s)

a:(t,s)

t\in\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}

\mathsf{id}_{t}:(t,t)

\alpha:(t,s)

\beta:(s,k)

\alpha;\beta:(t,k)

\alpha:(t_{1},s_{1})

\beta:(t_{2},s_{2})

\alpha\otimes\beta:(t_{1}\otimes t_{2},s_{1}\otimes s_{2})

\alpha:(t_{1},s_{1})

\beta:(t_{2},s_{2})

t_{1}:(T\mid S)

t_{2}:(S\mid K)

.

\alpha*\beta:(t_{1};t_{2},s_{1};s_{2})

Akin to terms, we denote the set of 2-terms by
\texttt{Term}^{2}_{\mathcal{L}}
.

Remark 3.15.

We have chosen not to extend the 2-terms to the recursively defined internal terms (i.e. the ones generated by the rules
and
). There is no inherent reason for omitting these terms: upon adding them, one would just need to add the corresponding structural 2-equations (see Definition
3.22
). However, in the models and the examples we will consider the 2-categorical structure only arises at the level of external terms, or does not need to be propagated between layers. Thus, for the sake of slightly reducing the complexity of the current presentation, we omit these terms. Moreover, as we shall observe in Corollary
4.4
, in deflational theories, such terms are automatically induced by the external ones.

Let
(F,F^{2}):(\mathcal{L},E^{0}_{\mathcal{L}},\eta_{\mathcal{L}})\rightarrow(\mathcal{K},E^{0}_{\mathcal{K}},\eta_{\mathcal{K}})
be a morphism between layered signatures with a choice of 2-cells. The functions between the generating 2-cells
F^{2}_{t,s}
then yield a function
F^{2}:\texttt{Term}^{2}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\texttt{Term}^{2}_{\mathcal{K}}
recursively defined as follows:

\displaystyle a:(t,s)

\displaystyle\mapsto F^{2}_{t,s}(a):(F(t),F(s))

\displaystyle\mathsf{id}_{t}:(t,t)

\displaystyle\mapsto\mathsf{id}_{F(t)}:(F(t),F(t))

\displaystyle\alpha\otimes\beta:(t_{1}\otimes t_{2},s_{1}\otimes s_{2})

\displaystyle\mapsto F^{2}(\alpha)\otimes F^{2}(\beta):(F(t_{1})\otimes F(t_{2}),F(s_{1})\otimes F(s_{2}))

\displaystyle\alpha;\beta:(t,k)

\displaystyle\mapsto F^{2}(\alpha);F^{2}(\beta):(F(t),F(k))

\displaystyle\alpha*\beta:(t_{1};t_{2},s_{1};s_{2})

\displaystyle\mapsto F^{2}(\alpha)*F^{2}(\beta):(F(t_{1});F(t_{2}),F(s_{1});F(s_{2})).

As for the terms, given a set of 1-equations
E^{1}
, a pair of 2-terms is in the
parallel 2-term relation

P^{2}_{\mathcal{L}}
with respect to
E^{1}
if and only if both 2-terms have the same sort up to the 1-equations:
\left(\alpha:(t_{\alpha},s_{\alpha}),\beta:(t_{\beta},s_{\beta})\right)\in P^{2}_{\mathcal{L}}
if and only if both
t_{\alpha}\overset{1}{=}t_{\beta}
and
s_{\alpha}\overset{1}{=}s_{\beta}
. We draw a 2-term
\alpha:(t,s)
either as

T
S
t
s
\alpha

, or simply as an arrow
t\xrightarrow{\alpha}s
(see e.g. Figure
10
on page
10
).

Proposition 3.16.

Let
(F,F^{2}):(\mathcal{L},E^{0}_{\mathcal{L}},\eta_{\mathcal{L}},E^{1}_{\mathcal{L}})\rightarrow(\mathcal{K},E^{0}_{\mathcal{K}},\eta_{\mathcal{K}},E^{1}_{\mathcal{K}})

be a morphism between layered signatures with a choice of 2-cells such that the induced function on terms
F:\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{K}}
preserves the specified 1-equations. Then the induced function on 2-terms
F^{2}:\texttt{Term}^{2}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\texttt{Term}^{2}_{\mathcal{K}}
preserves parallel terms: if
(\alpha,\beta)\in P^{2}_{\mathcal{L}}
, then
(F^{2}(\alpha),F^{2}(\beta))\in P^{2}_{\mathcal{K}}
.

Proof.

By the fact that 2-terms with the same sort are mapped to 2-terms with the same sort, and by induction on the construction of the term congruence.
∎

Definition 3.17 (2-equations).

Let
\mathcal{L}
be layered signature with a set of 0-equations
E^{0}
. Given a set of 1-equations
E^{1}
and a choice of 2-cells
\eta
with respect to
E^{0}
, a set of
2-equations
with respect to
E^{1}
and
\eta
is a subset
E^{2}\subseteq P^{2}_{\mathcal{L}}
.

Given a set of 2-equations
E^{2}
, we extend it to the
2-term congruence

\overset{2}{=}
, i.e. the smallest equivalence relation on
P^{2}_{\mathcal{L}}
containing
E^{2}
that is preserved by the recursive rules in Definition
3.14
.

3.3.
Theories and structural equations

We now have all the ingredients to define a layered theory.

Definition 3.18 (Layered theory).

Let us fix a recursive sorting procedure (Definition
3.10
). A
layered theory

(\mathcal{L},E^{0},E^{1},\eta,E^{2})
consists of the following: a layered signature
\mathcal{L}
(Definition
3.1
), a set of 0-equations
E^{0}
(Definition
3.8
), a set of 1-equations
E^{1}
with respect to
E^{0}
(Definition
3.12
), a choice of 2-cells
\eta
with respect to
E^{0}
(Definition
3.13
), a set of 2-equations
E^{2}
with respect to
E^{1}
and
\eta
(Definition
3.17
).

For a fixed recursive sorting procedure, a
morphism of layered theories

(F,F^{2}):(\mathcal{L},E^{0}_{\mathcal{L}},E^{1}_{\mathcal{L}},\eta_{\mathcal{L}},E^{2}_{\mathcal{L}})\rightarrow(\mathcal{K},E^{0}_{\mathcal{K}},E^{1}_{\mathcal{K}},\eta_{\mathcal{K}},E^{2}_{\mathcal{K}})

is given by a morphism of layered signatures with a choice of 2-cells
(F,F^{2})
(thus, in particular, the induced function
F:\texttt{Type}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\texttt{Type}_{\mathcal{K}}
preserves the 0-equations), such that the induced functions
F:\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\texttt{Term}^{1}_{\mathcal{K}}
and
F^{2}:\texttt{Term}^{2}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\texttt{Term}^{2}_{\mathcal{K}}
preserve the 1-equations and the 2-equations, respectively. We denote any category of layered theories by
\mathbf{LTh}
: note that each recursive sorting procedure results in a different category.

Proposition 3.19.

Let us fix a recursive sorting procedure. The forgetful functor
\mathbf{LTh}\rightarrow\mathbf{LSgn}
is a fibration. Moreover, the objects in the fibre
\mathbf{LTh}(\mathcal{L})
are precisely the layered theories with the signature
\mathcal{L}
.

Next, we define the structural equations that will hold in nearly all the models we will encounter, with the exception the “conditional box” notation defined in Subsection
, where we have to drop the functoriality requirement.

Definition 3.20 (Structural 0-equations).

Given a layered signature, the
structural 0-equations

S^{0}
are given by:

\displaystyle(AB)C:\omega

\displaystyle=A(BC):\omega,

\displaystyle\varepsilon A:\omega

\displaystyle=A:\omega=A\varepsilon:\omega,

\displaystyle f(AB):\tau

\displaystyle=f(A)f(B):\tau,

\displaystyle f(\varepsilon):\tau

\displaystyle=\varepsilon:\tau.

Definition 3.21 (Structural 1-equations).

Given a layered signature with the structural 0-equations (Definition
3.20
), the
structural 1-equations

S^{1}

the structural identities for monoidal theories (Definition
2.8
), where sequential composition is given by the rule

Definition 3.24 (Externally symmetric layered theory).

A layered theory is
externally symmetric
if it has the symmetry terms, and the structural 0-equations (Definition
3.20
) and 1-equations (Definition
3.21
) hold, and the 1-equations contain the equations for symmetric monoidal theories in Definition
2.10
for the symmetry terms.

Example 3.25.

Consider a layered theory
(\bullet,S^{0},E^{1},\varnothing,\varnothing)
with no generating 2-cells or 2-equations, where
\bullet
is a layered signature from Example
3.6
(one layer and no generators). The internal terms contain the terms of a monoidal signature (Definition
2.6
). If further
S^{1}\subseteq E^{1}
, then there is a one-to-one correspondence between the equivalence classes of internal terms and the equivalence classes of monoidal terms.

Example 3.26.

Consider a layered theory
(\omega\rightarrow\tau,S^{0},S^{1},\varnothing,\varnothing)
with no generating 2-cells or 2-equations, where
\omega\rightarrow\tau
is a layered signature from Example
3.6
(two layers with one generator between them). Then the internal terms with type
\omega
give the free monoidal category generated by the signature indexed by
\omega
, while the internal terms with type
\tau
give the free monoidal category generated by the disjoint union of the signature indexed by
\tau
and the generators obtained by the rule
. The 1-equations of Figure
4
then make
f:\omega\rightarrow\tau
a strict monoidal functor between the two free models. The functor is free in the sense that all the terms obtained by applying
f
to the internal terms with type
\omega
(the
rule) remain uninterpreted, and are simply added as generators to the monoidal category defined by the internal terms with type
\tau
.

We finish our abstract discussion of layered theories by defining three classes of layered theories that we will focus on: opfibrational, fibrational and deflational theories. In each case, we specify the recursive sorting procedure as well as the corresponding structural equations. In the case of deflational theories, we also define the structural 2-cells. In the sequel
(
lmt-part2
)
, we study models of these three classes of theories.

3.4.
Opfibrational, fibrational and deflational theories

Opfibrational theories are defined for the recursive procedure specified in Definition
3.27
and have no generating 2-cells.

Figure 6.
Rules for generating the opfibrational terms

Definition 3.27 (Opfibrational layered theory).

We say that a layered theory is
opfibrational
if it has no generating 2-cells, and its recursive sorting procedure consists of the rules in Figure
6
and the symmetry terms of Definition
3.23
(in addition to the basic terms in Figure
3
).

The intuition behind the opfibrational terms is that we take an “external” view of the monoidal categories and monoidal functors between them. In more detail:

•

the terms
and
capture the monoidal product and unit in the layer
\omega
: e.g. sliding the internal terms through the term
defines the monoidal product on morphisms (see Figure
7
),

•

the terms
capture the monoidal functors
f:\omega\rightarrow\tau
: any internal term appearing on the left-hand side of the boundary is in the domain
\omega
, and can be pushed through the boundary into the codomain
\tau
(see Figure
8
),

•

the terms
and
capture the cartesian monoidal structure of the category of monoidal categories; note that they do not correspond to any deleting or copying
inside
a layer, rather, it might be instructive to think of them as
branching
or
nondeterminism
:
represents branching into two potential histories of a system, while
corresponds to discarding one of the branches or histories.

Remark 3.28.

A more accurate name for the theories of Definition
3.27
would be a
strict layered theory for opfibrations with indexed monoids
. Since this is somewhat cumbersome, and we shall not consider any other layered theories featuring an opfibration, we stick to the term
opfibrational
.

We denote the resulting category of opfibrational layered theories by
\mathbf{OpFTh}
. In this case the morphisms are simply equation preserving morphisms of signatures rather than pairs of morphisms, as there are no generating 2-cells.

) for the terms

Figure 9.
Rules for generating the fibrational terms

The structural fibrational equations are likewise obtained by dualising the structural opfibrational equations (Definition
3.29
). For the sake of completeness, and since they will be used for defining the structural deflational equations, we state the definition explicitly.

Definition 3.30 (Structural fibrational equations).

By the
structural fibrational equations
we mean the structural equations, the external symmetry equations, as well as the following sets of 1-equations, where “dual” and “dualising” means reflecting the terms horizontally: (1) the equations of uniform monoids (the dual of Definition
2.13
) for the terms
and
, (2) the defining identities of monoidal categories obtained by dualising Figure
7
, and (3) the defining identities of monoidal functors obtained by dualising Figure
8
.

With these modifications, any properties of fibrational theories can be obtained by dualising the corresponding properties of opfibrational theories: all the diagrams are simply written in reverse direction.

We now arrive to our last – and most important – class of theories. Deflational theories can be thought of as glueing a pair of opfibrational and fibrational theories together along the internal terms.

Definition 3.31 (Deflational layered theory).

A layered theory is
deflational
if its recursive sorting procedure consists of the rules for the symmetry terms of Definition
3.23
, as well as of the rules for opfibrational and fibrational terms in Figures
6
and
9
(in addition to the basic terms in Figure
3
).

We denote the resulting category of deflational layered theories by
\mathbf{DeflTh}
.

In a deflational theory, every opfibrational term
x:(T\mid S)
generated by a rule in Figure
6
has a corresponding fibrational term
\bar{x}:(S\mid T)
generated by the corresponding rule in Figure
9
. We use this to define the
structural 2-cells
, expressing
\bar{x}
as the right adjoint to
x
.

Definition 3.32 (Structural 2-cells).

Given a deflational layered theory with layered signature
\mathcal{L}
, the
structural 2-cells
are given by the choice of 2-cells
\eta_{\mathsf{str}}
defined as follows: for every opfibrational term
x:(T\mid S)
generated by a rule in Figure
6
one has
\eta_{\mathsf{str}}\left(\mathsf{id}_{T},x;\bar{x}\right)\coloneq\{\eta_{x}\}
,
\eta_{\mathsf{str}}\left(\bar{x};x,\mathsf{id}_{S}\right)\coloneq\{\varepsilon_{x}\}
, and
\eta_{\mathsf{str}}
returns the empty set otherwise.

We display the 10 structural 2-cells explicitly in Figure
10
: the left-hand side contains the unit 2-cells (
\eta_{x}
), while the right-hand side contains the counit 2-cells (
\varepsilon_{x}
). We consistently omit the labels of the structural 2-cells, as the domain and the codomain determine them uniquely.

\blacktriangleleft_{f}
\vartriangleright_{f}
\blacktriangleleft_{f}
\vartriangleright_{f}

Figure 10.
Structural 2-cells for deflational theories

Definition 3.33 (Structural deflational equations).

By the
structural deflational equations
we mean: the structural opfibrational equations (Definition
3.29
), the structural fibrational equations (Definition
3.30
) and the following 2-equations for each opfibrational term
x:(T\mid S)
and all terms
y:(T\mid T)
and
z:(S\mid S)
that are either internal or a product (obtained by the
) of internal terms:

\displaystyle\left(\eta_{x}*\mathsf{id}_{x}\right);\left(\mathsf{id}_{x}*\varepsilon_{x}\right)

\displaystyle=\mathsf{id}_{x}

\displaystyle\left(\mathsf{id}_{\bar{x}}*\eta_{x}\right);\left(\varepsilon_{x}*\mathsf{id}_{\bar{x}}\right)

\displaystyle=\mathsf{id}_{\bar{x}}

\displaystyle\mathsf{id}_{y}*\eta_{x}

\displaystyle=\eta_{x}*\mathsf{id}_{y}

\displaystyle\mathsf{id}_{z}*\varepsilon_{x}

\displaystyle=\varepsilon_{x}*\mathsf{id}_{z}.

We denote the structural deflational 1- and 2-equations by
S_{\mathsf{defl}}^{1}
and
S_{\mathsf{defl}}^{2}
.

Note that the structural deflational equations contain, in particular, the structural 0-, 1- and 2-equations of Definitions
3.20
,
3.21
and
3.22
. The additional 2-equations that are required to hold are the usual zigzag equations defining an adjunction, as well as the equations stating the compatibility of the structural 2-cells with the “sliding through” 1-equations for internal terms in Figures
7
and
8
.

Given a deflational theory
\mathcal{T}
, let us write
\mathcal{T}_{\varepsilon}
for the theory obtained from
\mathcal{T}
by adding a section to each counit 2-cell in Figure
10
, i.e.
\kappa
such that
\kappa;\varepsilon=\mathsf{id}
. While
\mathcal{T}
and
\mathcal{T}_{\varepsilon}
are, in general, not equivalent as deflational theories, in
(
lmt-part2
)
we will show that they have the same (op)indexed monoidal categories as models. Since these are the main models of interest, in Sections
4
and
5
we will, therefore, make the assumption that the counits in Figure
10
have sections
\kappa
, as this will allow us to derive more properties within the formalism of deflational theories.

4.
Functor boxes and coboxes

Functor boxes
(or
functorial boxes
) extend the graphical syntax for monoidal categories (i.e. string diagrams) to monoidal functors. Given a monoidal functor
F:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}
, the idea is to draw a morphism
f:A\rightarrow B
in
\mathcal{C}
inside a box:

f
A
B
FA
FB

, which turns it into a morphism of type
FA\rightarrow FB
in
\mathcal{D}
. Thus, one may treat such boxes as terms composable with morphisms in
\mathcal{D}
. This idea extends to (co)lax monoidal functors. We refer the reader to the tutorial by Melliès
(
functorial-boxes
)
for the details.

In this section, we show that functor boxes arise naturally (and formally) within deflational theories. We will further observe that a box decomposes into the functor boundaries. Within our formalism, a functor box is, therefore, a derived notion rather than a primitive one. This flexibility allows for defining the dual notion, which we dub a
cobox
(Definition
4.6
), by composing the refinement and coarsening maps in the opposite order. While a box can be thought of as acting on its interior, a cobox can be thought of as acting on its exterior. Another intuition is to think of a cobox as a
window
(Definition
4.5
), allowing one to peak at the semantics (or at a finer level of granularity) of a part of a diagram.

This section provides the first examples of reasoning
within
layered theories. This is in contrast with the previous section as well as the sequel
(
lmt-part2
)
, which focus on proving properties
of
layered theories.

4.1.
Functor boxes

In any (op)fibrational or deflational theory, boxes are readily provided by the basic terms generated by the rule
. In deflational theories, boxes decompose into an internal term sandwiched between a coarsening and a refinement map, so that the term can slide out through either side of the box. We make this observation precise in Proposition
4.2
. We call a decomposed box a
cowindow
.

Definition 4.1 (Cowindow).

In a deflational theory, a 1-cell of the form

\blacktriangleleft_{f}
\vartriangleright_{f}
x

is called a
cowindow
, where
x
is any internal term.

We now make explicit the connection between cowindows and the usual notation for functor boxes.

Proposition 4.2.

In a deflational theory, there are bidirectional 2-cells

\blacktriangleleft_{f}
\vartriangleright_{f}
x
\kappa
\varepsilon
x
f

.

Proof.

The internal term
x
slides through
\blacktriangleleft_{f}
(or
\vartriangleright_{f}
) by the first equation in Figure
8
, after which we remove the fibrational-opfibrational generator pair by applying the counit
\varepsilon
(Figure
10
), which has a section
\kappa
.
∎

Note that in Proposition
4.2
, the term on the right-hand side is obtained by a rule for basic terms (Figure
3
), while the left-hand side is a composition of three terms in a deflational theory. Thus, functor boxes correspond directly to the terms on the right-hand side, while the proposition demonstrates that we can take one step further and decompose a functor box into three constituent parts. This implies that the standard functor equalities (Figure
4
) that had to be imposed in fibrational and opfibrational models are, in fact, provable in deflational theories:

Corollary 4.3.

In a deflational theory, the internal identities for monoidal functors (Figure
4
) are derivable from the external identities for monoidal functors (Figure
8
), up to a bidirectional 2-cell.

Proof.

We give the derivation of preservation of monoidal products below; other identities follow similarly:

Corollary 4.4.

In a deflational theory, the 2-cells recursively extend to all internal 1-terms.

Proof.

A 2-cell between internal terms
\alpha:x\rightarrow y
with sort
(A:\omega\mid B:\omega)
extends to

x
f
\blacktriangleleft_{f}
\vartriangleright_{f}
x
\mathsf{id}*\alpha*\mathsf{id}
\blacktriangleleft_{f}
\vartriangleright_{f}
y
y
f
\varepsilon
\kappa

for any
f\in\mathcal{F}(\omega,\tau)
. The extension to internal monoidal terms is similar, using the counit and its section.
∎

4.2.
Functor coboxes

In the definition of a cowindow (Definition
4.1
), there was no inherent reason to start with coarsening and end with refinement. The reason we chose this order of composition is to obtain the usual functor box: the internal term
x
is in the domain of
f
, while the whole term is in the codomain. Reversing the order of composition leads to the dual notion, a
cobox
, which, to the best knowledge of the authors, has hitherto not been studied abstractly, and has only appeared as a notational shorthand in string diagrammatic electrical circuit theory
(
electrical-circuits
;
boisseau-thesis
)
, which we make explicit as one of our case studies in Subsection
5.2
.

Unlike a box, a cobox does not correspond to any internal term, that is, there is no analogue of Proposition
4.2
for coboxes. Nonetheless, in many respects a cobox behaves as if it was an internal term, as we demonstrate in Proposition
4.8
. To do that, we need to separate the notion of a window (Definition
4.5
) from that of a cobox (Definition
4.6
), which allows some wires to bypass the window.

Definition 4.5 (Window).

In a deflational theory, a 1-cell of the form

\blacktriangleleft_{f}
\vartriangleright_{f}
x

is called a
window
, where
x
is any internal term.

A the level of syntax, a cobox is obtained by dualising the rule
for generating boxes. We then impose a 1-equation expressing the cobox as an existing term.

Definition 4.6 (Cobox).

Given a deflational theory, a
cobox
is a term generated by the rule

f\in\mathcal{F}(\omega,\tau)

A,B,C,D:\omega

Definition 4.7 (Symmetric deflational theory).

A deflational theory is
symmetric
if it contains the 1-equations for a symmetric monoidal theory (Definition
2.10
) for all internal terms for all layers, as well as the following isomorphic generating 2-cells:

\simeq

, together with the dual 2-cells obtained by horizontally reflecting the terms.

With Proposition
4.8
and the above identifications, the cobox may, in most cases, be treated as an internal term. One should, however, be aware that in reality it is not: for example, the cobox is, in general, not in the fibre of its domain category. One should also beware that while some identities that hold for boxes also hold for coboxes, in general, the box identities will not hold. We give some examples of this below.

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}
}.

Moreover, if (
4.12
) is an equality, then the implication (
4.13
) holds also when the bidirectional 2-cells on both sides are replaced with equalities (the converse does not hold in general).

5.
Case studies

Here we give extended examples of layered monoidal theories, boxes and coboxes. The examples with digital circuits (Section
5.1
), electrical circuits (Section
5.2
), ZX-calculus (Section
), and probabilistic channels (Section
) all build on monoidal theories from existing literature. We discuss how several levels of monoidal structure are used within existing work, and show how layered monoidal theories explicate and formalise such levels. In the remaining two examples, the calculus of communicating systems (Section
) and chemical reactions (Section
), the monoidal theories are constructed here for the first time in order to allow for a layered perspective.

The case studies are intended to be self-contained and independent of each other. At the beginning of each case study, we give a minimal introduction required to construct the layered theory at hand, and refer the reader to the literature for more details. It is certainly not necessary to read the case studies in order, nor are the details in any one of them required to understand the other examples.

5.1.
Digital circuits

We give a very simple example of an
arithmetic logic unit
(ALU) that is able to perform two operations on tuples of bits, the choice between which is controlled by one bit. To this end, we define the layered monoidal theory of
simple arithmetic circuits
with one layer for each
n\in\mathbb{N}_{+}
: the interpretation of logic and arithmetic gates within a layer is that they operate on
n
-bit wires. One benefit of our approach is that the monoidal signatures within each layer are nearly identical (a total of eight generators with arities and coarities in
\{0,1,2\}
), resulting in a rather compact definition. While the example ALU is very simple, the theory we define is expressive enough to represent an ALU for any computing circuit with arbitrary bitwise logic and arithmetic operations, such as a central processing unit (CPU).

In Kaye
(
kaye-thesis
, Example 3.20)
, the simple arithmetic circuits are introduced as the
generalised circuit signature for simple arithmetic circuits
, which is defined as an ordinary monoidal signature with an infinite number of colours (one for each number of bits
n\in\mathbb{N}_{+}
), and an infinite number of generators. The generators represent the same (finite) operations on bits as we define below in (
5.1
): an infinite number of generators is needed as their arities and coarities keep track of the number of incoming and outgoing wires, as well as the number of bits within each wire. In contrast, the layered theory presented here has a finite number of generators (eight) and colours (just a single one) in each layer, but there are now infinitely many layers (again, one for each number of bits).

Consider the following layered signature:
(\mathbb{N}_{+},\mathcal{F},\Sigma_{n})
, where for each
n\in\mathbb{N}_{+}
, the set
\mathcal{F}(n,1)
has exactly one element, and
\mathcal{F}
returns the empty set otherwise. For
n\neq 1
, the monoidal signature
\Sigma_{n}
is defined to have a single colour
n
, and the following monoidal generators:

(5.1)

We demonstrate the organisational power of layered theories by recasting Example 3.22 from Kaye
(
kaye-thesis
)
as a term in the theory of simple arithmetic circuits: we draw it on the left-hand side of Figure
12
. The term represents a simple ALU (arithmetic logic unit) operating on four bit wires with a one bit control wire: when the control bit is false, it performs bitwise AND, while when the control bit is true, it performs bitwise addition. We note that the labels
1
and
4
refer to the whole enclosed region, corresponding to the layers
n=1
and
n=4
. The layers are separated by a functor boundary labelled with
\vartriangleright
, corresponding to what is called a
bundler
in Kaye
(
kaye-thesis
)
. The translation from
4
-bit wires to
1
-bit wires can, therefore, be thought of as a bracketing, demarcating the two layers from each other. The formalism, however, allows for more than just separating different layers: using the equations within this layered theory, we observe that the term is equal to the one shown on the right-hand side. Note that while the functor boundary
\vartriangleright
“acts” from right to left, the overall logical flow of the diagram is from left to right.

5.2.
Electrical circuits

We formalise the notion of an
impedance box
, introduced in the study of compositional electrical circuit theory by Boisseau & Sobociński
(
electrical-circuits
)
and Boisseau
(
boisseau-thesis
)
. We find that it corresponds to a composition of a box with a cobox in a layered monoidal theory generated by translating electrical circuits to graphical affine algebra (Definition
). Within this deflational theory, we are able to replicate what is called the
impedance calculus
in
(
electrical-circuits
)
. To illustrate this, we derive the rule governing the sequential composition of resistors using our formalism. We summarise the layers we define in the table below:

\mathbf{ECirc}

The electrical circuits

\mathbf{Bip}

Bipole electrical circuits

\mathbf{GAA}

Graphical affine algebra: axiomatises affine relations

\mathbf{Imp}

All terms of
\mathbf{GAA}
with single input and output

Compositional electrical circuit theory
(
electrical-circuits
;
boisseau-thesis
;
compositional-networks
;
graphical-affine-algebra
)
treats the components of electrical circuits as generators in certain monoidal theory. The terms (string diagrams) in the theory bear very close resemblance to the electrical circuit diagrams in classical electrical circuit theory, and hence to the physical circuit. As formal mathematics, the diagrams allow for equational reasoning and a semantic interpretation as affine relations, bridging the gap between the physical wiring of the diagrams and proving their properties by the means of calculations. Our starting point is the work of Boisseau and Sobociński
(
electrical-circuits
)

Here
\mathbf{Bip}
is the layer of
bipoles
,
\mathbf{ECirc}
the layer of
electrical circuits
,
\mathbf{GAA}_{\mathbb{R}(x)}
the layer of
graphical affine algebra
over
\mathbb{R}(x)
, and
\mathbf{Imp}
is the
impedance layer
, consisting of all terms that may appear inside an impedance box (Definition
). We drop the subscript
\mathbb{R}(x)
for brevity, implicitly assuming that all the parameters in
\mathbf{GAA}
come from the field
\mathbb{R}(x)
.

Each of the four layers has exactly one colour. Following
(
electrical-circuits
)
, the wires and the generators in
\mathbf{ECirc}
and
\mathbf{Bip}
are coloured blue, while in
\mathbf{GAA}
and
\mathbf{Imp}
they are coloured black, however, this plays no formal role. The generators in
\mathbf{GAA}
are given by the generators of
graphical affine algebra
:
